defaults.hero.sub: From research and product strategy to interaction design and systems, I turn complex problems into products people can actually use.
defaults.work.label: Selected work
defaults.about.label: About
defaults.about.lead: At some point during lockdown I ran out of things to customise on my phone and accidentally became a product designer.
defaults.about.p1: The longer version involves a political science degree I don’t regret, a design certification I actually use, and five years of getting progressively more opinionated about hierarchy.
defaults.about.p2: These days I work on things that matter — fintech apps people check before coffee, AI tools they’re learning to trust, HR platforms they’re forced to open but shouldn’t have to hate. Enough industries to spot patterns. Enough humility to still run research.
defaults.cap.label: Capabilities
defaults.cap.lead: Six things I’m reliably good at.
defaults.cap.1.title: UX Strategy & Research
defaults.cap.1.body: I run user interviews, contextual field studies and usability testing, then turn the findings into journey maps, personas and a prioritised problem statement — so the roadmap is built on evidence rather than assumptions.
defaults.cap.2.title: Product & Interaction Design
defaults.cap.2.body: I design end-to-end product flows, information architecture and interaction models for web, tablet and mobile — covering the edge cases, empty states and error paths, not just the happy path.
defaults.cap.3.title: Design Systems
defaults.cap.3.body: I build and document scalable design systems in Figma — tokens, components, variants and usage guidelines — so engineering ships consistent, accessible UI faster and the visual language holds as the product grows.
defaults.cap.4.title: Visual & Interface Design
defaults.cap.4.body: I set typography, colour, spacing and layout systems that give an interface a clear hierarchy and a distinct brand voice, with every visual decision doing measurable work for comprehension.
defaults.cap.5.title: AI & Emerging Technology
defaults.cap.5.body: I design for AI-assisted and agentic products — prompt and result patterns, confidence and citation cues, review and override controls — so users understand what the system did and stay in control of the outcome.
defaults.cap.6.title: Collaboration & Delivery
defaults.cap.6.body: I work alongside product managers, engineers and QA from discovery to release: annotated specs, design reviews, developer handoff in Figma and post-launch iteration based on analytics and user feedback.
defaults.contact.label: Contact
defaults.contact.title: Got something to build, or something to fix?
defaults.contact.sub: I have opinions — especially about the thing you can’t quite put into words yet. That’s usually where the good work starts.

kriyam.name: Kriyam.ai
kriyam.statRest: Faster Verifications with zero data leaks…
kriyam.lede: End-to-end field investigation — dispatch, track, collect, verify.

facts.v: Senior User Interface & User Experience Designer
Insurance & NBFCs, Operations & Compliance and Verfication Agencies

impact.p: Unstructured phone calls and WhatsApp dispatches were replaced with structured digital workflows—making case assignments instant and eliminating delays across every step.
Standardised forms and guided inputs removed reliance on manual data entry—significantly improving accuracy and reducing time spent on corrections.
All customer data is processed within a secure, encrypted environment—eliminating untracked sharing through intermediaries and ensuring full regulatory compliance.
Every action is automatically logged, giving teams complete transparency and audit readiness—without manual record-keeping.

overview: Insurance FCUs, TPAs, and investigation agencies operate in a high-stakes environment where every manual error, every undetected fraud, and every data leak carries direct financial and regulatory consequences. With crores lost annually to insurance fraud in India, IRDAI mandates around data protection tightening, and FCU teams stretched thin, the need for a structured, compliant verification process was not optional — it was critical.

Before Kriyam.ai, field verification was entirely ad-hoc. Cases were dispatched over phone calls, WhatsApp, and emails — with no traceability, no SLA control, and no audit trail. Customer personally identifiable information was being shared with agencies through unencrypted channels, creating serious regulatory exposure. Document forgery — tampered IDs, deepfake photos, fabricated certificates — went undetected because manual reviewers lacked the tools to catch what automated systems can flag in seconds. The result was a process riddled with inefficiency, liability, and compliance gaps.

To address this, I led the design of Kriyam.ai — a comprehensive web and mobile field verification platform built to replace these unsecured, untraceable workflows. The platform introduced location-traced case assignments, end-to-end encrypted data handling, and full auditability, bringing the entire verification process into compliance with India's DPDP Laws. By eliminating informal channels entirely, every verification became structured, accountable, and legally defensible.

The impact was immediate and measurable. Turnaround time dropped by 30%, reported errors fell by 80%, and data leakages reached zero. AI-powered case summarisation now saves clients 12 hours of work weekly, and overall productivity for field verification teams has tripled. Kriyam.ai transformed what was once an uncontrolled liability into a reliable, efficient, and fully compliant operation — giving agencies real control over their data and their risk.
role: As the Senior UI/UX Designer, I partnered closely with the product manager, a dev lead, a UI Designer, three developers, and a QA engineer to shape Kriyam.ai from concept through launch. My process was deeply collaborative and iterative, not linear.

The product manager identified the features we needed to build. From there, I took ownership of research and discovery — understanding the user context, mapping workflows, and designing the simplest, fastest, most user-friendly path to solve each problem.

Rather than handing off finished designs, I maintained continuous dialogue with the development team throughout their build process, reviewing their work, offering insights, and iterating together as implementation revealed new considerations.

Once features moved to QA, issues and edge cases came back to me for refinement. I worked closely with the QA team to understand what was breaking or confusing, and we'd refine both the design and implementation to fix it.

This constant feedback loop — product defining features, me designing and researching, developers building with my input, QA validating and flagging issues — became the rhythm that shaped how Kriyam.ai came together.

proteger.name: Proteger Collect
proteger.statRest: faster data capture with zero friction on the factory floor.
proteger.lede: End-to-end operational intelligence for manufacturers. Designed with factory workers, built for speed.

facts.v:
Web Application, Tablet &
Mobile Application (iOS & Android)
Factory Owners, Floor Workers, Maintenance Teams, QC, Operations Leadership

impact.p: Voice and vision based inputs eliminate manual entry friction. Factory workers capture data in seconds, not minutes, even in challenging conditions.

impact.h: 15 minutes saved per shift per worker
impact.p: Hands-free operation means workers spend less time on paperwork, more time on production. That's genuine productivity gain across your entire floor.
Predictive maintenance alerts mean issues are caught before machines fail. Maintenance teams respond faster. Factory keeps running.
Digital capture with AI validation removes human transcription mistakes. No more illegible notes or misplaced data.

overview: When we first stepped onto the factory floor, the reality hit hard. These weren't office workers with ideal conditions. Factory workers were battling poor lighting, wearing heavy gloves, safety helmets, and protective gear that made interaction with standard devices genuinely difficult. They were drowning in paperwork — maintenance logs written by hand, quality checks scribbled on clipboards, material tracking spread across scattered notebooks. This wasn't inefficiency born from laziness. It was a system fundamentally misaligned with how people actually worked.

We spent weeks on the floor, talking to workers one-on-one, watching them struggle. A maintenance technician trying to fill a form with thick gloves on. A quality inspector squinting in dim lighting to read small text. A line supervisor manually cross-referencing batch numbers across three different sheets. The pain points weren't subtle — they were baked into every interaction.

That's when the vision for Proteger crystallised. Not a generic factory app, but a suite purpose-built for real factory conditions. We started with Protegal Collect, our voice and vision-first data capture layer. But designing for gloved hands and poor visibility meant rethinking everything. Button sizes had to expand. Check sheets needed restructuring for large gloved fingers. Typography had to account for harsh overhead lighting and helmet-shadowed vision.

But the tablet was always meant to be a bridge, not the destination. The real target was voice. Hands completely free. No device to fumble with, no gloves fighting touchscreens. Just speak, and the system understands. We're building that future now — integrating advanced voice recognition and AI that learns factory-specific terminology, machine names, process jargon. Workers can stand at a machine, dictate maintenance notes, and data flows directly into the system.

Alongside Collect, we built Trace for material and batch tracking, giving full traceability through the production line. Then came the maintenance module — intelligent work management that predicts when machines need attention before they break. Quality management built on real-time digital records, not paper audits. And Analytics pulling everything together into live dashboards that give managers sight across the entire operation.
role: As UI and UX Designer on Proteger, my responsibility spanned the entire user experience across the suite — from initial research through design refinement and ongoing feature development. Our team conducted extensive user research directly on factory floors, visiting production facilities and conducting one-on-one interviews with maintenance technicians, quality inspectors, line supervisors, and equipment operators. I synthesised those insights into design principles that shaped every interface decision.

I owned the design of Proteger Collect, our voice and vision-first data capture layer, ensuring every button size, interaction pattern, and voice flow accounted for real factory conditions — poor lighting, gloved hands, safety gear constraints. I worked closely with the development team to translate those constraints into thoughtful solutions: accessibility-first interface design and the foundational voice architecture we're now building toward.

Across the full Proteger suite, I ensured cohesion — that Trace, the maintenance module, quality management, and Analytics all felt like one unified system rather than disconnected tools. My focus throughout was keeping the factory worker at the centre of every decision, designing not around their limitations but in respect of their reality.

The work wasn't unconstrained creativity. I navigated genuine boundaries throughout the project. Time constraints meant prioritising features that had the highest impact on factory operations. Enterprise compliance and regulatory requirements shaped how data flowed through the system and where it could be stored — everything needed to remain secure within internal infrastructure with zero external data leakage. Design language consistency had to bridge multiple modules while maintaining accessibility standards. These weren't obstacles to work around. They were conditions that made the design more rigorous, more honest, and ultimately more useful to the people using it every day.

goodbook.name: Goodbook
goodbook.lede: A comprehensive HR and attendance platform built for office-based workforces. Intelligence at the point of interaction.

facts.v: HR Departments, Finance Teams, Employees, Office Management.

impact.p: Facial recognition eliminates physical card dependency. Employees check in across office locations instantaneously, with liveness detection preventing spoofing.
Automated payroll generation and instant employee access to digital payslips removes the administrative overhead that previously consumed HR bandwidth.
AI-powered liveness detection and automated cross-referencing eliminate manual entry errors and buddy punching. The system is effectively tamper-proof.
End-to-end automation from check-in through payslip generation compresses what previously took days into hours. Finance and HR teams operate at genuine scale.

overview: The modern office HR function is drowning in process. HR teams manually reconcile attendance sheets. Finance teams spend days generating payslips from spreadsheets. Employees chase HR for paperwork. Check-in systems built around physical keycards create unnecessary friction — lost cards, slow queues, no actionable data. For small to mid-sized organisations with up to 250 employees, this overhead is particularly acute. Every hour spent on payroll administration is an hour away from strategic HR work.

Our research mapped the actual workflows. Employees wasted time fumbling with expired keycards or waiting in queues. HR spent disproportionate effort manually generating payslips — a repetitive, error-prone monthly ritual. Finance couldn't trust attendance data without manual verification. Office managers lacked visibility into who was present, creating scheduling complications. The system treated attendance as a compliance box to tick rather than business intelligence to act on.

Goodbook unified the entire employee lifecycle. We started with Gate Pass, our facial recognition check-in layer designed specifically for office environments. This wasn't novelty. We implemented liveness detection using AI and machine learning, requiring employees to perform specific randomised actions — smile, blink, turn to light. This prevents spoofing via image or video, ensuring attendance records remain trustworthy at scale. For office spaces with multiple entry points, this became the single source of truth for who is present and when.

The mobile application became the employee hub. Real-time attendance visibility. Leave management with granular categorisation — earned leave, casual leave, compensatory leave, maternity leave — with clear progress indicators showing remaining balance. Asset tracking showing company devices assigned to them. Expense submission for reimbursement. Critically, manual attendance adjustment when check-in failures occurred, eliminating the email-to-HR friction that previously consumed days of back-and-forth.

For HR teams, we built a comprehensive web platform. Complete administrative control over employee records, shift assignment, and policy management. Automated payslip generation connected to salary processing — the moment salary deposits, payslips are immediately available for employee download. Historical access to payslips across years and months. Company policies centralised and searchable. Real-time dashboards showing attendance patterns and compliance metrics.

Multi-location support meant that organisations with multiple office locations or flexible work arrangements had complete visibility. Geolocation tracking identified where employees were checking in from — office, home, or designated client location. For smaller teams managing hotdesking or hybrid arrangements, this provided the intelligence needed to optimise space and resources.

The design philosophy was straightforward: remove friction, not introduce it. Every feature traced back to a specific pain point. Every interaction was optimised for its context. The result was a system that gave HR teams back their time and gave employees clarity over their own employment data.
role: As UI/UX Designer, I led the complete product experience across three distinct platforms: the employee mobile application, the HR web platform, and Gate Pass facial recognition layer. Each platform served fundamentally different users in different contexts, demanding simultaneous attention to contrasting design requirements.

My process began with structured research across stakeholder groups — HR teams, finance, and employees across office locations. I mapped existing workflows, identified where administrative friction accumulated, and anchored every design decision in observable reality rather than assumption.

For the mobile experience, I designed with speed and clarity as the primary constraints. Employees needed immediate access to attendance status, leave balances, payslips, and expense submission without navigation overhead. For the HR web platform, the demands inverted — depth and control were necessary, with payroll automation, audit trails, and compliance dashboards designed for power users who needed to process data at scale.

Gate Pass required a distinct approach. Liveness detection needed to feel intuitive despite its sophistication — randomised action sequences delivered through clear on-screen instructions with real-time feedback, ensuring daily adoption without friction. I worked closely with the machine learning team to shape this interaction model end to end.

Throughout, data integrity and security shaped design decisions — access controls, audit visibility, and geolocation presentation were considered at interface level, not delegated to engineering. The full product was delivered within a compressed six-month timeline through disciplined prioritisation and rapid iteration with real users.
